title: The house that sailed round the Horn

place.label: Stanyan House, 2006 Bush St at Buchanan

hook: Five years into the Gold Rush, a New England house arrived by ship and was set down beside a toll road. It is still here.
story:
When this modest house went up at Bush and Buchanan in 1854, Bush Street was still a toll road and the Gold Rush was only five years old [1]. Many prefabricated houses were shipped to San Francisco from New England in the Gold Rush years. This "Boston House" is one of the few that has been positively identified as having come around Cape Horn [1].

Its first occupant was Charles Stanyan, who later sat on the city's Board of Supervisors from 1866 to 1869 and served on the committee that chose the site for Golden Gate Park [2]. Stanyan Street, which runs along the park's eastern edge, carries his name [2]. The house stayed in the Stanyan family for more than a hundred years [1], and it is the oldest surviving house in this part of the city.

The city made it Landmark No. 66 [3]. It is still a private home, a little wooden survivor of the frontier town, standing among the Victorians that came later.

title: The last cow in the Western Addition

place.label: Ortman-Shumate House, 1901 Scott St at Pine

hook: A German grocer bought a huge lot in 1870. His family held on for more than a century, and so, for a while, did the family cow.
story:
On 25 February 1870, John Frederic Ortman bought this unusually large lot at Scott and Pine [1]. He was born in Germany in 1829, came to California in 1851, and started out as a grocery clerk before running his own grocery business. A few years after moving here he retired, and the 1876 city directory lists him simply as a "Capitalist" [1].

Before 1890 Ortman owned the whole block frontage from California to Pine, and in the 1890s he built houses for his two daughters when they married [1]. The family also kept a cow. When Emerson School took a neighbouring lot for its new concrete building in the 1920s, the Shumate cow lost its pasture. The city's landmark report calls it "one of the last, if not the very last" privately owned cow in the Western Addition [1].

The Italianate house stayed with the builder's descendants. When it became Landmark No. 98 in 1977, Dr. Albert Shumate, the first president of the city's Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board, was still living here [1][2].

title: A wedding gift paid for in sealskins
hook: This Italianate mansion was a father's wedding present. The money behind it came from fur seals on remote Alaskan islands.
story:
In 1876 Louis Sloss built this Italianate house, with Stick-style touches, as a wedding present for his daughter Estelle and her husband, Ernest L. Lilienthal [1]. The Slosses lived nearby, and their friends the Wormsers built the house next door [1].

Sloss had started out dealing in mining stocks, and he saw an opportunity in Alaska. After the United States bought the territory from Russia in 1867, he and his partners bought out the old Russian-American Company, and in 1868 they reorganised it as the Alaska Commercial Company [2]. The firm won a federal concession to harvest seal skins on two Alaskan islands, and the landmark report says that concession "netted him a large fortune" [1]. So one of Pacific Heights' finest Victorians was built on the fur trade of the far north.

In 1907 the Lilienthals sold the house to Orville C. Pratt Jr., whose family ran a large ranch near Chico. His widow Emily lived here until 1953. In 1955 the Bransten family bought it, which kept together a row of four Victorian mansions and their gardens [1].

title: The Atherton women of California Street

place.label: Atherton House, 1990 California St at Octavia

hook: A strong-willed Chilean widow, a restless young novelist, a husband who never came home and, later, a woman with fifty cats.
story:
Dominga de Goñi Atherton was a Chilean widow whose husband, Faxon Atherton, had made his fortune in Valparaíso and then bought a large estate in San Mateo County. In 1881 she built this eccentric Queen Anne and Stick-Eastlake house at California and Octavia [1][2]. Her son George and his wife Gertrude moved in with her. Gertrude found life under her mother-in-law stifling and began to build an independent life. Her first serial story appeared in The Argonaut in 1882 under the pen name "Asmodeus" [3].

In 1887 George sailed for Chile and died at sea [2][3]. House lore has it that his body came home preserved in a barrel of rum [2]. Left to support herself, Gertrude published her first novel in 1888 and went on to a long career as a writer [3].

After Dominga died in 1890 the house was sold [1]. In 1923 the architect Charles J. Rousseau divided it into 13 apartments, and his widow Carrie lived here with fifty cats until 1974 [1]. Ghost-hunters say the house is haunted, which may be the most Pacific Heights ending of all [2].

title: Where Stanford's medical school was born

place.label: Cooper Medical College site, Sacramento & Webster Sts

hook: For 77 years, Stanford trained its doctors on this corner of Pacific Heights, not in Palo Alto.
story:
In 1858 Dr. Elias Samuel Cooper founded the first medical school on the West Coast, in a building on Mission Street [1]. When he died in 1862 the school faded. His nephew, Levi Cooper Lane, revived it in 1870, and in 1882 he gave it a new building at Webster and Sacramento streets, renamed Cooper Medical College [1]. Lane went on to add a hospital, a nursing school and the endowed Lane Medical Library [1].

Dr. Charles Ellinwood, a Civil War surgeon who founded the Marine Hospital in the Presidio, taught physiology here and later became the college's president [2]. In 1908 Cooper Medical College was given to Stanford University, and it became Stanford's medical department. The school did not move to the Palo Alto campus until 1959 [1].

The original building, described as a "Dickensian Gothic structure," was torn down around 1970 [2]. Albert Pissis's Classical Revival library of 1912 still stands at 2395 Sacramento, and it is now city Landmark No. 115 [3].

title: A ferry captain's farmhouse
hook: A captain who logged over a million miles on 18-minute bay crossings retired to an old dairy farmhouse, and built himself a ship's cabin in the garden.
story:
Set back from Pacific Avenue among the mansions is one of the oldest houses in San Francisco. It was probably built around 1853 as the main house of a dairy farm, though historians disagree about exactly when it went up [1][2].

From the 1880s until 1964 it belonged to the family of Captain John Leale. Sources disagree on the date: NoeHill says he bought it in 1883, while the Bloomfields date the family's ownership from 1886 [1][2]. Leale spent 34 years as a San Francisco Bay ferry captain. In his memoir, Recollections of a Tule Sailor, he counted more than 125,000 round trips and over a million miles, on crossings scheduled to take 18 minutes [2]. His daughter Marian remembered him as "punctilious, spartan, commanding" [2].

The family added the porch, bay windows and rear extension between 1899 and 1913 [2]. In retirement the captain entertained friends at the back of the garden in a replica ship's cabin made from parts salvaged from old vessels, porthole included [1][2]. The farmhouse remains, surrounded by the city that grew up around it.

title: First firehouse with a three-horse team

place.label: Old Engine Company No. 23, 3022 Washington St

hook: In the horse-drawn era, this plain wooden firehouse sent out the city's first three-horse hitch, racing to fires from the Richmond to the bay.
story:
In June 1893 the city approved plans for three new firehouses by Henriksen and Mahoney. The architect Bernhardt E. Henriksen was praised in 1884 as "the pioneer native born architect" [1]. This one, on Washington Street between Broderick and Baker, is now one of only two of the three still standing [1].

Engine Company No. 23 was organised in 1894. A 1902 report lists its equipment: a third-class La France engine and a Graves hose wagon carrying 750 feet of two-inch hose. Its crew answered alarms across the Richmond District and the whole area west of Laguna, between Geary and the bay. It was the first house in the Fire Department to use a three-horse hitch [1]. The horses were replaced by engines in 1915 [1].

The building stayed a firehouse until 1963. Then John Dickinson bought it and turned it into a studio and home, and by 1970 many of its missing exterior details had been restored [1]. The city lists it as Landmark No. 93 [2].

title: A Venetian palace for the Lovers of Peace

place.label: Bush Street Temple (Ohabai Shalome), 1881 Bush St

hook: Wood made to look like Sienese marble, minarets and Venetian arches: San Francisco's third Jewish congregation built itself a palace on Bush Street.
story:
On 15 September 1895, exactly thirty years after it consecrated its first temple on Mason Street, Congregation Ohabai Shalome ("Lovers of Peace") dedicated this new home on Bush Street [1]. The architect, Moses J. Lyon, borrowed from Venice. A loggia of seven arches with delicate tracery recalls the Ca' d'Oro or the Doge's Palace, and the wooden front was painted to imitate Sienese marble. There were seats for a thousand people. Tall minarets once rose from the towers, and Judaic symbols, including the tablets of the Ten Commandments, filled the space between them [1].

The congregation was one of the most conservative in the city [2]. Many of its neighbours were Jewish merchant families, most of them of German background. A census study of the 1700 block of Bush in 1900 found cigar importers, clothing wholesalers, clerks and Rabbi Jacob Nieto of Sherith Israel living a block away [2]. The temple later became a centre for Zionist causes [1].

As membership waned, the building was sold in 1934 to a group of Japanese Soto Zen Buddhists. It later housed the early San Francisco Zen Center, before becoming part of a senior home [1].

title: A church built like a forest

place.label: Swedenborgian Church, 2107 Lyon St at Washington

hook: Bark-covered madrone trunks hold up the roof, and the chairs were made without a single nail. It was a manifesto of California's Arts and Crafts movement.
story:
The Reverend Joseph Worcester came to San Francisco from Boston in 1867 to lead a congregation of followers of the mystic Emanuel Swedenborg. At first they worshipped in Druids Hall on Sutter Street [1]. In 1894 Worcester began planning a church of his own at Lyon and Washington, working with a remarkable group of friends [1][2].

The painter Bruce Porter sketched an Italian village church he had seen near Verona. A young draughtsman in A. Page Brown's office, Bernard Maybeck, drew up the plans [1]. The church, finished in 1895, brings nature indoors. Massive madrone logs, their bark still on, support a heavy tile roof. The maple chairs were made by hand without nails, and their seats were woven from tule rushes gathered in the Sacramento River Delta. Even the walled garden was planted with symbolic meaning [1].

It is considered one of California's earliest pure Arts and Crafts buildings [2]. In 2004 it was named a National Historic Landmark [1][2], and it is still in use as a church.

title: Mary Ellen Pleasant's house at Octavia and Bush

place.label: Mary Ellen Pleasant Memorial Park, Octavia St at Bush

hook: The eucalyptus trees on Octavia are all that remain of the mansion of a Black entrepreneur and abolitionist whom the city's gossip papers turned into a villain.
story:
Mary Ellen Pleasant arrived in San Francisco in 1852 and became one of its most remarkable figures [1]. She helped fugitives escape slavery, invested in mining and banking alongside her partner Thomas Bell, and in 1866 was thrown off a streetcar with two other Black women [2]. Her lawsuit, Pleasant v. North Beach & Mission Railroad, reached the California Supreme Court, which ruled segregation on streetcars unlawful, although it overturned her $500 in damages [2][3].

For the last two decades of her life she lived in a 30-room mansion at Bush and Octavia, which she had paid to build [2]. After Bell died in 1892, his widow Teresa accused Pleasant of stealing from the estate. In 1899 Pleasant left the house for a six-room apartment on Webster Street [2]. She died in 1904, having lost most of her fortune [1].

Newspapers spread lurid tales of "Mammy" Pleasant and voodoo. Historians such as Lynn Hudson have since shown how much of that story came from gossip sheets [1]. The eucalyptus trees she planted still stand here as Mary Ellen Pleasant Memorial Park, said to be the smallest park in the city [2].

title: A church rebuilt from a million bricks

place.label: Calvary Presbyterian Church, 2501-2515 Fillmore St at Jackson

hook: Calvary took its Union Square church apart and rebuilt it on Fillmore, bricks, pews and all. Four years later it was sheltering congregations and even a courtroom.
story:
Calvary Presbyterian was founded on 23 July 1854. Its first church on Bush Street, between Montgomery and Sansome, was then the largest Protestant church on the West Coast. As business crowded in, the congregation moved in 1869 to Powell and Geary on Union Square [1].

At the turn of the century it moved west again, to Fillmore and Jackson, and it brought its old church along. About one million bricks from the Union Square building went into the new church, with all the pews, the metal balcony supports and much of the woodwork [1]. The first service was held on Thanksgiving Day 1902, and the church was dedicated on 7 February 1904 [1].

The move proved timely. After the 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed downtown, St. Luke's Episcopal, Old First Presbyterian and Temple Emanu-El all held services here, and a temporary Superior Court courtroom ran in the basement [1]. The city's landmark report notes that the church's interior of around 1900 has seen "almost no unsympathetic change" [2].

title: A dome that rode out the quake

place.label: Temple Sherith Israel, 2266 California St at Webster

hook: A Gold Rush congregation moved west in 1905. Seven months later the earthquake struck, and its great domed temple barely noticed.
story:
Congregation Sherith Israel was founded during the Gold Rush, and it is one of the oldest synagogues in the United States [1]. From 1868 it worshipped downtown at Post and Taylor, but like many of the city's Jewish families it moved west to the Western Addition [2]. Its rabbi, Jacob Nieto, lived on Bush Street [2].

For the new temple at California and Webster, the congregation hired Albert Pissis, who was trained at the École des Beaux-Arts. The cornerstone was laid on 22 February 1904, and the temple was consecrated on 24 September 1905 [3]. It blends Byzantine and Romanesque forms and rises 140 feet, under a dome 60 feet across. Its organ has 3,500 pipes [1].

Seven months later the 1906 earthquake struck. The temple suffered only modest damage, which was quickly repaired, while the fire destroyed downtown [1][3]. According to the congregation's history, the synagogue then became a principal site of the city's graft prosecution trials, in which political boss Abe Ruef and his allies faced corruption charges [3]. It came through the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake undamaged as well [3].

title: The night the fire reached Franklin Street
hook: Soldiers dynamited the mansions of Van Ness Avenue to stop the fire. By dawn the flames had reached Franklin Street, and the Haas family's house survived.
story:
On the evening of 19 April 1906 the great fire reached Van Ness Avenue. On the orders of Colonel Charles Morris, army troops dynamited the mansions along the avenue to create a firebreak [1]. By 5 a.m. on 20 April the fire had burned as far as Franklin Street, then turned south [1]. The destruction largely stopped at Van Ness, and most of the Western Addition, including the new mansions of Pacific Heights, was left unburned [2].

One block west of Van Ness, on Franklin between Washington and Jackson, stood the Queen Anne house that architect Peter R. Schmidt had designed in 1886 for William Haas, a Bavarian-born wholesale grocer [3][4]. It survived the earthquake and the fire [4]. The Haas family's daughter Alice and her husband, Samuel Lilienthal, moved in in 1917, and Alice lived here until her death in 1972 [3].

In 1973 her heirs gave the house to the new Foundation for San Francisco's Architectural Heritage, now San Francisco Heritage [3][4]. Today SF Heritage looks after it, a grand Victorian that stood at the very edge of the 1906 fire.

title: When Fillmore became downtown
hook: With downtown in ashes, City Hall and the big Market Street stores moved to Fillmore. For a few years a neighbourhood shopping street was the heart of the city.
story:
The 1906 fire stopped short of Fillmore Street. Within days of the earthquake, City Hall and most of the big Market Street department stores had moved into whatever space they could find along it [1]. The first streetcar to run again after the disaster ran on Fillmore [1].

Photographs from 1906 show Fillmore, looking north from Sutter to Bush, as the city's busiest shopping district [2]. Around the corner on Bush Street, between Fillmore and Steiner, families cooked in the street on wood-burning stoves [2]. Single-family Victorians nearby were turned into boarding houses, and the Western Addition quickly became a densely populated urban district [1][3].

The boom did not last. As downtown was rebuilt, the stores moved back [3]. In 1909 Fillmore merchants tried to keep their customers by hanging fourteen brightly lit arches over the street's intersections, and Fillmore was soon being called "the most highly illuminated thoroughfare in America" [1].

title: Alma's château on Washington Street
hook: The daughter of poor Danish immigrants married a sugar heir and got a French Baroque palace, but she insisted the Victorians on the site be saved, not torn down.
story:
Alma de Bretteville was born in San Francisco in 1881, the fifth of six children of Danish immigrants [2]. Adolph Spreckels, heir to his father Claus's sugar empire, courted her for five years. They married on 11 May 1908, when he was 24 years older than she was [1][2]. (The popular story that she posed for the Dewey Monument in Union Square is disputed. An article from 1902 names a different model [2].)

For their home, Adolph bought and combined several lots on Washington Street with views of the bay and the Golden Gate. George Applegarth, trained at the École des Beaux-Arts, designed the French Baroque mansion, which was completed in 1912 [1][2]. Alma refused to let the existing houses be demolished. Six Victorians on Jackson Street and two on Washington were moved instead [1].

She went on to collect Rodin and had Applegarth design the California Palace of the Legion of Honor. It opened on 11 November 1924, six months after Adolph's death [1][2]. Alma lived in the mansion until she died in 1968 [1].

title: A home when the YWCA said no

place.label: Madame C.J. Walker Home for Girls, 2066 Pine St

hook: Barred from the YWCA, Black women arriving in San Francisco found rooms, jobs and a Christmas street party at an Italianate house on Pine Street.
story:
In 1921 this Italianate house of 1878-79 on Pine Street became the Madame C.J. Walker Home for Girls. It was named after the cosmetics entrepreneur often described as the first African American woman to become a millionaire [1][2]. The home was opened by Irene Bell Ruggles, president of the California State Federation of Colored Women's Clubs, with financial support from Third Baptist Church [2].

It met a real need. Black women new to the city were not eligible to use the YWCA's services, and although the Chinese and Japanese communities had their own YWCA branches by the 1910s, there was no branch for Black women in San Francisco [1][2]. "There being no colored YWCA in the city," an account from around 1920 said, "the Home must perform to some extent the duties of a 'Y'" [1]. Single women found lodgings and job referrals here. The social hall and large kitchen, with a basement hall added in 1926, hosted community gatherings [1][2]. Every Christmas "the block is roped off so that the children may safely enjoy the games dancing and music" [1].

The home ran until 1972 and became city Landmark No. 211 in 1999 [2].
